app.subtitle: Local IP reputation analysis, URL scans, DMARC reports and AbuseIPDB reports
app.lang_switch_confirm: Changing the language reloads the page and discards unsaved work (a running analysis or pasted text). Continue?
about.description: A local tool for IP reputation analysis, URL scanning, DMARC reports and preparing AbuseIPDB abuse reports. It runs locally only (127.0.0.1), with no login and without sending anything out except:
about.outbound_1: explicit queries to the selected threat-intel services, once the API keys are provided
about.outbound_2: one IP address sent to ipwho.is on an explicit click of the "geo/ASN" button in the DMARC tab
about.outbound_3: explicit analyses performed by an LLM through OpenRouter, once the API key and the model are defined
about.name_meaning: a Japanese word meaning a thorough, detailed examination - looking at something closely. Pronounced roughly "say-sah".

lookup.subtitle: Check the reputation of an IP address in several independent threat-intelligence sources at once (VirusTotal, AlienVault OTX, Cloudflare Radar, AbuseIPDB, GreyNoise, WHOIS/rDNS) and see one aggregate risk score.
lookup.batch_hint: Paste IP addresses, one per line
urlscan.subtitle: Submit a live scan of a suspicious URL to urlscan.io - you get a detailed report on the page content, network traffic, detected technologies and verdict without opening the link yourself.
urlscan.no_uuid: urlscan.io did not return a scan identifier.
urlscan.submitted: Scan submitted - waiting for the result...
urlscan.still_running: The scan is still running after {time} - check manually
urlscan.hint.unlisted: Unlisted: the scan is hidden from the urlscan.io front page and public search, but stays visible to verified security researchers in urlscan Pro. User agent: default. Scan country: automatic.
urlscan.hint.private: Private: the scan is visible only to your urlscan.io account (it counts against the separate private-scan quota). User agent: default. Scan country: automatic.
urlscan.hint.public: Public: the scan and the scanned URL appear on the urlscan.io front page and in public search - anyone can see them. Do not use it for addresses that contain personal data or tokens.
urlscan.full_pending: urlscan.io does not return this scan any more (or it is still running).
usr.copy_title: Copies the address in a defanged form (hxxp, [.])
usr.note_unknown: urlscan.io has no verdict for this page yet. That does not mean it is safe.
usr.note_low: No malicious signals in the urlscan.io data. That is not a guarantee - a fresh phishing page often has no verdict yet.
usr.cert_new_title: A certificate issued in the last week is typical for freshly set up phishing sites
usr.shot_caption: Screenshot rendered by urlscan.io - your browser did not visit the scanned page. Click to enlarge.
usr.thumb_caption: Thumbnail saved with the scan. Click to enlarge.
usr.shot_missing: urlscan.io has no screenshot for this scan.
usr.f.title: Page title
usr.f.cert_age: Age on the day of the scan
usr.d_verdict: Malicious score, categories, brands the page imitates, and the verdicts of antivirus engines and the community.
usr.clipped: Showing the first {shown} of {total}; the rest is in the full API response.
urlscan.existing_none: urlscan.io has no earlier scans of this domain.
urlscan.existing_note: The list contains public scans by anyone plus the scans of your urlscan.io account, newest first. Open one instead of ordering a new scan when it is recent enough.
usr.b_form: a password form posts to another domain or over plain HTTP
usr.note_form: urlscan.io has no strong verdict, but the page has a password form posting elsewhere - Seisa rates it at least Medium.
usr.d_forms: Forms found in the rendered page (only the structure is read, nothing from the page is loaded). A password field that posts to another domain is a typical phishing kit.
em.f.scan_title: Put this address into the URLScan tab (nothing is opened or scanned until you click Scan there)
md.service.virustotal: Detection ratio from antivirus engines, reputation, ASN, categories, tags and WHOIS.
md.service.otx: Number and names of threat-intel pulses linked to this indicator, geolocation, ASN.
md.service.cloudflare: Network/context data - ASN, location, routing. This is not a reputation verdict.
md.service.abuseipdb: Abuse confidence score, number of reports, author of the latest report, ISP, usage type.
md.service.greynoise: Whether the address is known 'internet noise' (mass scanners/bots) or something unusual.
md.service.whois: WHOIS record of a domain or reverse DNS (PTR) of an IP address - a direct protocol query, with no external account and no single source website.
dmarc.subtitle: Upload aggregate DMARC reports (XML, also packed as .gz or .zip) from mail providers to see which servers send messages on behalf of your domain, whether they pass SPF/DKIM and their alignment, and which IP addresses look suspicious.
dmarc.drop_multiple: You can upload several reports at once; .xml, .gz and .zip files are accepted
dmarc.no_auth_data: no auth_results/{section} data in this record
dmarc.no_records: No records to display in the selected files.
dmarc.banner_bad_one: {n} source fails both SPF and DKIM ({messages}).
dmarc.banner_bad_other: {n} sources fail both SPF and DKIM ({messages}).
dmarc.banner_bad_detail: {ips}. Rejected: {reject}, quarantined: {quarantine}, delivered untouched: {none}. Check whether these are legitimate senders missing from your SPF/DKIM setup or someone spoofing your domain.
dmarc.banner_warn_one: {n} source fails SPF or DKIM on some messages - DMARC can still pass through the other method.
dmarc.banner_warn_other: {n} sources fail SPF or DKIM on some messages - DMARC can still pass through the other method.
dmarc.banner_good: All sources pass both SPF and DKIM.
dmarc.legend_spf: Checks whether the sending server's IP address is authorised in the SPF record of the envelope-from (Return-Path) domain. auth_results is the raw result (pass, fail, softfail, neutral, none, temperror, permerror) with the domain and scope (mfrom or helo); policy_evaluated says whether it also matched the From domain (alignment) and so counts for DMARC.
dmarc.legend_dkim: Checks the cryptographic signature the sending server added to the message (the d= domain and the s= selector). auth_results is the raw signature result; policy_evaluated says whether the signing domain matched the From domain and so counts for DMARC.
dmarc.legend_policy: p is what receivers should do with mail that fails DMARC: none (only report), quarantine (spam folder), reject (refuse). sp is the same for subdomains, pct the share of messages the policy applies to, adkim/aspf the alignment (relaxed allows subdomains, strict needs an exact match), fo the failure-report options, np the policy for non-existent subdomains. Decision is what the receiver actually did and can differ from p because of an override. A message passes DMARC when SPF or DKIM passes and is aligned.
dmarc.err_no_unpack: this browser cannot unpack archives - unpack the file and load the .xml
dmarc.err_too_large: the unpacked report is too large
dmarc.err_archive: the archive could not be read
dmarc.hint_none_ready: {domain}: p=none only monitors, and every source in these reports passes - the policy can likely be tightened to quarantine, then reject.
dmarc.hint_none_risky: {domain}: p=none only monitors, so messages from suspicious sources are delivered untouched. Fix legitimate senders first, then tighten the policy.
dmarc.hint_quarantine_ready: {domain}: p=quarantine and every source in these reports passes - the policy can likely be tightened to reject.
dmarc.hint_pct: {domain}: pct={pct} - the policy applies to only {pct}% of failing messages, the rest is handled with a milder action.
dmarc.legend_table: The SPF and DKIM counts in the sources table are the policy_evaluated results (after alignment), not the raw auth_results. A source can therefore show SPF as failed although auth_results says pass for another domain - typical for forwarded mail, which receivers often mark with an override such as forwarded or mailing_list.
rb.subtitle: Paste the raw source of a suspicious e-mail to prepare and submit an abuse report to AbuseIPDB - with automatic fact extraction, optional AI analysis and full control over the content before sending.
rb.llm_banner: The content is sent to OpenRouter/Claude Sonnet for analysis only after you click "Analyze". "Analyze without LLM" sends nothing off this computer.
rb.info_only: The items below are informational only - they do not block sending. Verify them yourself before clicking "Send".
rb.attachments_summary: Detected attachments ({n}) - taken into account by the AI in the report comment
rb.llm_full: The model saw the complete message source (headers and the whole body, {chars} characters).
rb.not_qualifying: This e-mail most likely does NOT qualify for a report.
rb.qualifying: The e-mail looks eligible for a report.
rb.llm_failed: The LLM analysis failed ({error}) - showing the rule-based result only.
rb.ai_other_ip: The AI suggests a different IP address than the one detected automatically.
rb.ai_ip_hint: This is only a suggestion - verify it manually in the Received chain below and correct the IP field in Step 2 if needed.
rb.check.received_verified: Verified from the Received header (not From/body)
rb.check.not_spoofed_source: The source is trustworthy (established TCP/SMTP connection)
rb.needs_llm: Requires AI analysis - add an OpenRouter key to .env and use "Analyze".
rb.note.received_ok: The address was taken from the Received header.
rb.note.no_email_auto: No e-mail pasted - cannot be assessed automatically.
rb.note.spoofing_detected: Detected - SPF or DMARC returned fail ({state}). You can select the Spoofing category.
rb.note.spoofing_none: Not detected - the sender passed authentication ({state}). Do not select the Spoofing category.
rb.note.spoofing_nodata: Cannot be assessed - the pasted source has no SPF/DKIM/DMARC results (no Authentication-Results; the receiving server may not have added them, or they were dropped when pasting). Select Spoofing only if you can confirm it another way.
rb.note.spoofing_unclear: Cannot be assessed - the results are ambiguous ({state}). Select Spoofing only if you can confirm it another way.
rb.self_sent_title: Most likely does NOT qualify for a report (local assessment).
rb.self_sent_body: The message looks like a test sent from your own account to yourself ({address}): the sender, the envelope sender and the recipient are the same address, and the headers show no sign of an attack (no SPF/DMARC fail, attachments or ransom demand). No model has read the content - use "Analyze" to confirm.
rb.hard_only_body: Without AI analysis only the hard criteria were checked: a public IP address and an age of up to 60 days. That is not enough to say the e-mail is worth reporting - use "Analyze".
rb.ip_info: AbuseIPDB (90 days): {reports} reports from {users} users, confidence score {score}%, last report {date}.
rb.ip_info_none: AbuseIPDB (90 days): no reports of this address so far.
rb.cooldown: You already reported this address a moment ago. AbuseIPDB accepts the next report of the same IP only after 15 minutes - about {minutes} min left.
rb.prev_reports: You have already reported this address {n} time(s) with Seisa, last on {date}.
rb.llm_blocked: The AI analysis disputed the item above - sending is blocked. Check the Received chain and run "Analyze" again after correcting the data.
em.subtitle: Paste the full source of an e-mail (headers + body) or load an .eml file and Seisa breaks it down: first it shows hard facts computed locally (Received route, authentication, domain alignment, timeline, MIME structure, links, hidden content), then a language model walks through a detailed analysis of both the good and the bad elements - step by step, so you learn to read the source of a message.
em.banner: The whole message (with headers) is sent to OpenRouter for analysis after you click "Analyze". The message is treated as untrusted text: nothing in it is opened or downloaded and the links in the results are not clickable.
em.dup_banner: This message was already analysed on {date} ({details}). Open the saved analysis instead of paying twice, or run the analysis again{more}
em.prep_notes: Preparing the source for the model: {notes}.
em.no_key: No OpenRouter key (OPENROUTER_API_KEY in .env) - showing the deterministic analysis only.
em.model_writing: The model is writing the analysis...
em.aborted: Cancelled - the incomplete analysis was not saved.
em.citations_ok: Citation check (local, free): {n} items checked (IP addresses, quoted headers, SCL/BCL values, identifiers) and all match the source.
em.citations_bad: Citation check: {bad} of {n} checked items do not match the source.
em.citations_hint: This is not always an error (it may be an example, a paraphrase or an abbreviation), but check these places before treating them as true:
em.truncated_banner: The analysis was cut off by the response length limit - its final parts are missing.
em.continuing: The model is writing the missing parts...
em.f.title: Deterministic analysis
em.f.md_intro: Computed locally by Seisa, without a language model. URLs are defanged.
em.f.no_flags: No anomalies were detected automatically (that does not mean there are none).
em.f.received: Message route: Received headers ({n}), from the top (newest)
em.f.received_help: Trust boundary: only the Received header added by the recipient's server is reliable. The roles below are a code heuristic; the final assessment is made by the analysis.
em.f.auth_count: Authentication: SPF / DKIM / DMARC / ARC ({n} result headers)
em.f.auth_help: Only the Authentication-Results written by the recipient's server (authserv-id) counts. A result written by anyone else is just their claim.
em.f.filters: Recipient's anti-spam filters and flags set by the sender
em.f.filters_help: The filter headers were written by the recipient's server (they carry evidential weight). The sender's flags are its own claims - not proof, only an element of pressure or tracking.
em.f.opaque: Headers unreadable for humans (internal Microsoft blobs)
em.f.epochs: Epoch timestamps found in the headers
em.f.html: HTML content: links, remote elements, hidden content
em.f.wrapped_anchor: Large part of the content wrapped in a single link
em.f.dup_headers: Repeated headers that should appear only once
em.f.casing: Different letter case in header names (trace of different programs)
em.f.intro: Computed locally by Seisa, without a language model: these are hard facts extracted from the source. The model receives them as input.
em.x.title: E-mail analysis: {subject}
em.x.truncated: Note: the LLM analysis was cut off by the length limit (the final parts are missing).
em.x.citations_ok: Checked {n} items (IP addresses, quoted headers, SCL/BCL values, identifiers): all match the source.
em.x.citations_bad: {bad} of {n} checked items do not match the source (not always an error: an example, a paraphrase, an abbreviation):
em.saved_empty: No saved analyses. Every completed analysis is saved together with the raw e-mail in the data/analyses directory.
em.dup_other_lang: That analysis is in a different language than the interface; a new analysis in {ui} is paid (a cost similar to the previous one).
em.lang_notice: This LLM analysis was written in {lang}, while the interface is in {ui}. The text of the analysis and the facts stay in the language they were created in (the interface labels are in {ui}).
lookup.agreement_title.single: Only one source reports this field, so there is nothing to compare.
lookup.agreement_title.agree: All sources that report this field give the same value.
lookup.agreement_title.majority: The sources disagree; the value shown is the one most of them report. Click for the other values.
lookup.agreement_title.conflict: The sources disagree and none has a majority; the value shown comes from the highest-priority source (the registry, RDAP, first). Click for all values.
lookup.raw_summary: Stored summary (the raw response is not kept in history)
lookup.nothing_more: Nothing more to show here; see the full API response.
lookup.f.name: Name
lookup.legend.score: One number 0-100 combined from the sources that voted (noisy-OR model): agreeing sources reinforce each other, a strong signal is not averaged away and a source without data does not vote. Below {medium} is low, from {medium} to below {high} is medium, {high} and above is high. A known good IP (AbuseIPDB whitelist, GreyNoise benign/RIOT, OTX validation) is capped at {cap} unless another source has a strong contradicting signal.
lookup.legend.risk: How dangerous one source considers the address, 0-100, on a scale chosen for what that service measures. Credibility is the largest share of that vote that counts, because the sources are not fully independent (VirusTotal absorbs part of the same reports as AbuseIPDB).
lookup.legend.signal: A source with a source risk of {medium} or more counts as a signal: its card opens automatically and its jump link is amber. Other cards stay closed but hold the same details.
lookup.legend.identity: ASN, owner, country and network merged from every source that reports them, after normalising the values. Badges: ✓ all sources agree, ≈ a majority agrees (click for the other values), ⚠ no majority, 1 source means there is nothing to compare.
lookup.legend.priority: On a tie the value of the highest-priority source is shown: RDAP (the registry itself) first for owner, network and contact, VirusTotal first for ASN. The priority never overrides a majority, and the identity never changes the score.
lookup.legend.country: The registration country (RDAP: where the address block was registered) and the geolocation country (where the address appears to be) are separate fields. They often differ for hosting, anycast and leased ranges, which is normal.
lookup.legend.confidence: AbuseIPDB: how sure it is that the address is abusive, based on the reports of the last 90 days weighted by the trust in the reporters. It is not a count of reports.
lookup.legend.greynoise: GreyNoise: malicious = seen attacking, benign = a known harmless scanner or service, unknown = seen but not classified. Noise means mass internet scanning, not necessarily an attack aimed at you.
lookup.legend.riot: GreyNoise list of common business services (CDNs, clouds, search engines). An address on it is expected to look noisy and is treated as known good.
lookup.legend.pulses: AlienVault OTX: community threat reports that mention the address. Fresh, enriched pulses (adversary, malware family, ATT&CK) count more than old bulk lists, and OTX alone never gives a high score.
lookup.legend.whitelisted: AbuseIPDB: the address is on its allow list (known good), so its source risk is 0.
